anchor: Pallas Athene gave might and courage
title: Aristeia: the 'excellence' of Diomedes
short: Book V opens the first aristeia of the Iliad, a sequence in which one hero, inspired by a god, dominates the battlefield and wins kleos.
body: An aristeia (from aristos, 'best') is a stretch of narrative in which one warrior, filled with divine menos ('might'), outshines everyone else. Athena's gift here leads to the stated goal: that Diomedes should be 'pre-eminent' and 'win glorious renown' (kleos esthlon, 5.3). Monro notes the same pattern for Agamemnon (Book XI), Patroclus (XVI) and Menelaus (XVII). The ancient title 'Aristeia of Diomedes' is old: Herodotus (2.116) cites lines from Book VI under that name, so the episode was known as a unit by the fifth century BC and ran on into Book VI. Leaf observes that Diomedes here outdoes anything Akhilleus does, and many analysts (Leaf among them) thought the book was built up from an independent Diomedeia; Monro argued instead that Book VI presupposes Book V in its present place. Diomedes, obedient to Athena, serves as a stand-in for the absent Akhilleus; compare 5.788-91, where Hera says the Trojans never left their gates while Akhilleus fought.

title: The 'star of harvest-time' (Sirius)
short: The 'star of harvest-time' is Sirius, the Dog Star, whose late-summer rising brought heat and fever; the fire on Diomedes' armour is both glorious and deadly.
body: Opōrinos means 'of opōra', the late summer when fruit ripens, not our autumn. LSJ and Monro identify the star as Sirius, as the parallel at 22.26-31 makes clear: there Priam sees Akhilleus racing over the plain 'like the star of harvest-time' called 'Orion's dog', brightest of stars but 'a sign of evil' that brings fever to mortals. The star 'bathed in Ocean' is one newly risen out of the river that rings the earth. Leaf suggests the flame Athena kindles on Diomedes' helmet and shield is 'a symbol of invincible fury' rather than a physical fire, since no one in the story remarks on it; compare the flame Athena lights around Akhilleus' head at 18.205-14. Readers of Book XXII will see that the same image marks Akhilleus at the start of his last fight, so Diomedes is once again cast as Akhilleus' substitute.

title: Ares 'bane of mortals, blood-stained, stormer of walls'
greek: Ἆρες Ἄρες βροτολοιγὲ μιαιφόνε τειχεσιπλῆτα (Ares Ares brotoloige miaiphone teichesiplēta)
short: A whole line of insulting epithets for the war god: 'plague of men, blood-stained, approacher of walls'.
body: Athena's address to Ares packs three epithets into one hexameter. Brotoloigos is 'plague' or 'ruin of mortals' (LSJ); miaiphonos is 'stained with blood (of murder)'; teichesiplētēs, from pelazō 'come near', is literally 'one who comes up against walls', hence 'stormer of cities' (LSJ; Monro). Apollo repeats the line at 5.455. The doubled vocative 'Ares, Ares' gives the line an exasperated, almost mocking tone. The epithets set up Book V's portrait of Ares as the least lovable of the gods: he switches sides (5.831-4), bellows when wounded, and Zeus calls him 'most hateful' of the Olympians (5.890). Leaf calls him an Olympian swashbuckler, while Diomedes 'typifies all the nobler qualities of pious heroism'.

title: Phereclus and the ships 'that began the evil'
short: Phereclus built Paris' ships for the voyage to Sparta; the rare word archekakos marks them as the 'beginning of evils' for Troy.
body: The victim Phereclus is a craftsman whose name and ancestry advertise his trade: his father is Tecton ('Carpenter'), his grandfather Harmon ('Joiner'), so, as Leaf notes, the craft is hereditary over three generations. He built the ships that carried Paris (Alexander) to Helen. LSJ glosses archekakos as 'beginning mischief'; the Iliad uses it only here. Leaf points out that Herodotus clearly had the line in mind when he said that the twenty Athenian ships sent to the Ionian revolt were 'the beginning of evils for Greeks and barbarians' (Hdt. 5.97). The poet adds that Phereclus did not know the 'oracles of the gods' (5.64): skill in making things, taught by Athena, did not bring knowledge of what was fated.

title: Simile: Diomedes as a winter torrent
greek: ποταμῷ πλήθοντι ἐοικὼς χειμάρρῳ (potamōi plēthonti eoikōs cheimarrōi)
short: Diomedes sweeps across the plain like a river in winter flood that bursts the dykes and ruins the farmers' work.
body: A cheimarros is a torrent swollen by winter rain or melting snow. Leaf explains the gephyrai, which Murray renders 'embankments', as dykes along the banks rather than bridges, the usual Homeric sense of the word, and the 'walls of the vineyards' as field fences. The simile turns the aristeia into a natural disaster: the flood is driven by 'the rain of Zeus', and 'the fair works of men' (erga, here the tilled fields) fall before it. The lines just before it (5.85-6) make the same point another way: no one could tell which army Diomedes belonged to. Virgil imitates the passage for the sack of Troy, where a foaming river bursts its banks and carries off herds and stalls (Aeneid 2.496-9); Leaf cites the imitation. Compare the smaller torrent simile at 4.452-6, where two armies meet like rivers in winter flood.

anchor: the mist moreover have I taken
title: Athena lifts the mist from Diomedes' eyes
greek: ἀχλὺν δ᾽ αὖ τοι ἀπ᾽ ὀφθαλμῶν ἕλον (achlun d' au toi ap' ophthalmōn helon)
short: Athena removes the 'mist' (achlus) that normally keeps mortals from recognising gods, so that Diomedes can tell god from man.
body: Ordinary mortals cannot see gods for what they are; Athena takes away the achlus (mist, darkness) on Diomedes' eyes so that he can 'well discern both god and man'. The gift comes with a rule: he must not fight any immortal except Aphrodite. Much of the book tests this rule: he wounds Aphrodite (5.335-40), attacks Apollo three times (5.436-42), retreats before Ares (5.596-606), and finally wounds Ares with Athena beside him (5.855-9). Monro lists these god-fighting passages and notes that the theme runs into Book VI. Leaf calls Diomedes' claim at 6.128-9 that he would not fight gods one of the most glaring contradictions in the poem. Virgil adapts the scene when Venus clears Aeneas' sight to show him the gods destroying Troy (Aeneid 2.604-6), and Monro contrasts Virgil's elaborate sentence with Homer's directness.

title: Simile: the wounded lion in the sheepfold
short: Wounded but not stopped, Diomedes returns three times as fierce, like a lion grazed by a shepherd that then ravages the unguarded flock.
body: The simile answers Pandarus' arrow (5.95-100): the wound only makes Diomedes fiercer, his rage 'thrice so great'. Monro reads the scene as a shepherd in lonely country who finds the lion leaping into the fold, grazes it, and then retreats in fear into the farm buildings while the lion works its will on the sheep. Leaf discusses the awkward grammar of 5.140-2 and reports Bayfield's view that 5.141-2 may be an addition; he admits the simile is more effective without them but notes that epic style likes to tell the fate of the sheep. The point of comparison is the reversal: the wound meant to stop the predator makes it more dangerous. Lion similes cluster around Diomedes in this book (compare 5.161-4, the lion breaking the neck of a heifer); Leaf quotes a hunter's observation that a lion kills cattle in just that way.

title: 'The next of kin divided his goods' (inheritance)
greek: χηρωσταὶ δὲ διὰ κτῆσιν δατέοντο (chērōstai de dia ktēsin dateonto)
short: When an old man loses his only sons, distant relatives (chērōstai) inherit; the line shows what the death of young warriors means for families at home.
body: Xanthus and Thoon are the only sons of the aged Phaenops, so their deaths leave him with 'lamentation and grievous sorrow' and his property passes to the chērōstai. Leaf glosses the rare word as 'inheritors of the bereaved father', the next of kin or distant relatives, and notes that it occurs elsewhere in early poetry only at Hesiod, Theogony 606-7, where the man who avoids marriage dies without a son to care for him in old age and distant kin divide his estate. Leaf adds that we do not know whether, in the Homeric world, unclaimed property went to the family or the wider community. The vignette is typical of the Iliad's 'obituaries' for minor victims: a few lines open onto a household and a future that the battle destroys. Compare the sons of the dream-interpreter Eurydamas just before (5.148-51).

title: The horses of Tros, payment for Ganymede
short: Aeneas' horses descend from the divine horses Zeus gave King Tros to pay (poinē) for taking his son Ganymede.
body: The 'horses of Tros' (5.222) are the finest breed 'beneath the dawn and the sun'. Diomedes explains their pedigree: Zeus gave them to Tros as poinē, a compensation or blood-price, for his son Ganymede, whom the gods carried off to be Zeus' cup-bearer because of his beauty (told at 20.231-5). Anchises secretly put his mares to Laomedon's stallions and so obtained six foals, two of which he gave to Aeneas. The Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite (202-17) tells the same story of Ganymede and the compensating horses. Tros is the eponymous ancestor of the Trojans, and Leaf and Monro explain the adjective Trōïoi (5.222) as 'of the breed of Tros'. The horses become a prize: Sthenelus captures them at 5.319-27, and they reappear at 8.105-8 under Diomedes' control. The same theft and payment explains why Laomedon's mares matter in the Tlepolemus episode (5.640).

title: 'Such as mortals now are': the shrinking of men
greek: οἷοι νῦν βροτοί εἰσ᾽ (hoioi nun brotoi eis')
short: The narrator contrasts the heroes with present-day men: Diomedes lifts alone a stone that two men of the singer's own time could not carry.
body: This is one of the rare places where the narrator steps outside the story to compare its world with his audience's. Leaf notes that the phrase occurs four times in the Iliad (here, 12.383, 12.449, 20.287) and never in the Odyssey; compare Nestor's boast that the men of his youth were mightier than any now alive (1.271-2). The idea that the heroic age was a race of stronger men is also in Hesiod's myth of the ages (Works and Days 156-73). The stone strikes Aeneas at the hip-joint, which Homer pauses to name: kotylē, 'the cup', the word men use for it. LSJ gives kotylē as a cup and, by extension, the socket of the hip; Leaf compares the Latin anatomical term acetabulum. The precise anatomy is typical of Iliadic wounding scenes and sets up Aphrodite's rescue.

title: Cypris (Aphrodite) wounded
short: 'Cypris', 'the Cyprian', is Aphrodite's title in this episode only; Diomedes wounds her because she is an analkis, 'unwarlike', goddess.
body: Monro and Leaf both note that the Iliad calls Aphrodite Kupris only in Book V (5.330, 422, 458, 760, 883). Her cult centre at Paphos on Cyprus is mentioned in the Odyssey (8.362-3). Leaf argues that the name does not imply a belief in her Cyprian origin, since Book V makes her the daughter of the old goddess Dione, and Aphrodite in Homer is a full Olympian with no visible Near Eastern features; scholars still debate how far she derives from the Phoenician Astarte. Diomedes picks her out because she is analkis, 'without strength in war', unlike Athena or Enyo. The scene is a pointed piece of divine comedy: the spear pierces the robe 'the Graces themselves had wrought', Diomedes taunts her about 'beguiling weakling women', and Zeus finally tells her that war is not her business (5.428-30). Her rescue of Aeneas recalls her rescue of Paris at 3.373-82.

title: Enyo, 'sacker of cities'
short: Enyo is a goddess of battle-slaughter, paired with Ares; she appears in Homer only in Book V.
body: Enyo is named only twice in Homer, both in this book. Here she stands with Athena as a goddess who 'lords it' in war, the opposite of Aphrodite. At 5.592-3 she leads the Trojans alongside Ares, 'bringing ruthless Din of War' (Kydoimos). Leaf notes that Kydoimos ('uproar, tumult') seems to be another personification, like those on the aegis (5.739-40) and on Akhilleus' shield (18.535), and that the phrase may mean she has him as her attendant or carries him like a weapon; Monro prefers the second reading, with Kydoimos as a thing in Enyo's hands just as the spear is in Ares'. Her epithet ptoliporthos, 'sacker of cities', is otherwise given to heroes such as Akhilleus and Odysseus. Homer also calls Ares Enyalios (e.g. 2.651), a name apparently from the same root, and Roman writers identified Enyo with Bellona.

title: Ichor, the blood of the gods
short: Ichor is the bloodless fluid in the veins of gods, who 'eat not bread neither drink wine' and so are immortal.
body: The poet explains that what flows from Aphrodite's wrist is not blood but ichor, because gods do not eat bread or drink 'flaming wine' and are therefore 'bloodless' and called immortal. LSJ defines ichor as 'the juice, not blood, that flows in the veins of gods', citing this line; in later Greek the word means the watery serum of blood or a discharge from wounds, and Aeschylus uses it simply for blood (Agamemnon 1480). The idea links diet and mortality: men are 'eaters of bread', and the gods live on ambrosia and nectar. Leaf, however, judged 5.340-2 a 'very poor interpolation', since ichor occurs elsewhere in Homer only at 5.416 and later poets did not adopt the special sense; and Ares, wounded later, is said to bleed 'immortal blood' (5.870). Readers should therefore treat the theology here as a single, possibly late, explanation rather than a fixed Homeric doctrine.

title: Dione, mother of Aphrodite
short: In the Iliad Aphrodite is the daughter of Zeus and Dione, not the foam-born goddess of Hesiod.
body: Dione appears only here in Homer. Making her Aphrodite's mother gives the goddess an ordinary Olympian parentage (daughter of Zeus, 5.131), whereas in Hesiod's Theogony (188-206) Aphrodite is born from the sea-foam around the severed genitals of Ouranos. Plato's Symposium (180d-e) later combines the two accounts into a 'heavenly' Aphrodite, motherless child of Ouranos, and a 'common' one, daughter of Zeus and Dione. Leaf regards Dione as a very old goddess, worshipped beside Zeus at Dodona, and connects her name with Latin Diana (both are usually derived from the root of Zeus' own name); Hesiod lists her among the daughters of Ocean (Theogony 353). Her speech of consolation (5.382-415) is a short catalogue of gods who suffered at mortal hands, a typical paradeigma (mythological example) used to comfort.

title: Otus and Ephialtes imprison Ares
greek: Ὦτος κρατερός τ᾽ Ἐφιάλτης, παῖδες Ἀλωῆος (Ōtos krateros t' Ephialtēs, paides Alōēos)
short: Dione's first example: the giant sons of Aloeus kept Ares chained in a bronze jar for thirteen months until Hermes stole him away.
body: The Aloadae, Otus and Ephialtes, were giant brothers who tried to pile Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa to reach heaven; their story is told in the Odyssey (11.305-20) and by Apollodorus (Library 1.7.4), who also mentions their binding of Ares. Leaf notes that the bronze keramos recalls the enormous storage jars found at Hissarlik, made of bronze here because divine things are made of precious materials, and that the thirteen months are a lunar year. The point for Aphrodite is simple: even Ares, 'insatiate of war', nearly perished at mortal (or semi-mortal) hands. The stepmother Eëriboea's betrayal of her stepsons is a small folk-tale touch.

title: Heracles wounds Hera and Hades 'in Pylos among the dead'
greek: ἐν Πύλῳ ἐν νεκύεσσι (en Pulōi en nekuessi)
short: Heracles shot Hera and even Hades; whether 'Pylos' is the city or 'the gate' of the underworld was disputed in antiquity.
body: Dione's next examples involve Heracles, 'son of Amphitryon' and archer (Monro notes that in Homer he is still mortal and an archer; the club is later). He wounded Hera with a three-barbed arrow and Hades 'in Pylos among the dead'. Aristarchus took pulos as a form of pulē, 'gate', so that Hades was shot at the gate of the underworld; Leaf and Monro both prefer the place-name, linking the story to Heracles' attack on Pylos recalled by Nestor (11.689-93). Pindar has Heracles fight Poseidon, Apollo and Hades at Pylos (Olympian 9.29-35), and Pausanias (6.25.2-3) explains a yearly-opened precinct of Hades at Elis as thanks for the god's help to the Pylians, quoting these very lines. Leaf suggests that Pylos may have been thought of as a gate of Hades, so both senses could be in play. Paeon then heals Hades (5.401).

title: Paeon, healer of the gods
short: Paeon is the gods' physician, who heals Hades and later Ares by spreading 'pain-killing drugs' on their wounds.
body: Paiēōn heals Hades here and Ares at 5.899-904 with odunēphata pharmaka, herbal remedies that 'slay pain' (Murray's 'simples' are medicinal herbs). Leaf notes that Homer mentions him only in these passages and at Odyssey 4.231-2, where the Egyptians, skilled in drugs, are called 'of the race of Paieon'; he appears to be a separate god, not Apollo, who in Homer has no healing role apart from 16.514-29. In later Greek the name became a title of Apollo as healer, and the paean (paiēōn), the hymn sung in Book I (1.472-4) to end the plague, is named after the same figure. The formula 'for he was in no wise of mortal mould' (5.402, 5.901) reminds us that immortals cannot die of wounds, only suffer pain.

title: Athena's joke and Zeus' verdict: 'the works of marriage'
short: Athena mocks Aphrodite for scratching her hand on a brooch; Zeus smiles and assigns her the 'lovely works of marriage', leaving war to Ares and Athena.
body: Athena's taunt imagines Aphrodite seducing an Achaean woman to follow the Trojans and scratching her hand on the woman's golden brooch. Leaf notes that the brooch (peronē) is the pin of the Doric peplos fastened at the shoulder, and he calls the taunt close to 'chaff', joking talk that may allude to the abduction of Helen. Zeus' reply sets out the division of divine spheres: war belongs to Ares and Athena, desire and marriage to Aphrodite. The scene shows the Homeric gods at their most human and comic, a contrast with the suffering they cause on earth; Leaf and other analysts regarded 5.418-30 as a late addition because of this light tone. Diomedes' attack on a god outside her sphere is thus both a heroic feat and a category mistake, as Apollo points out in the next scene.

anchor: like of spirit with the gods
title: 'Thrice he leapt... the fourth time': the limit between gods and men
greek: μηδὲ θεοῖσιν ἶσ᾽ ἔθελε φρονέειν (mēde theoisin is' ethele phroneein)
short: Apollo stops Diomedes' fourth charge with the Iliad's clearest statement that gods and men are of different races and must not be equated.
body: The pattern 'three times... but when for the fourth time he rushed on like a god (daimoni isos)' recurs at the climaxes of Patroclus' aristeia (16.702-11, 16.784-6) and Akhilleus' fight with Hector (20.445-54); Leaf collects the parallels. Each time a god intervenes and the hero meets a limit. Apollo's warning states it directly: never is the 'tribe' (phulon) of immortal gods like that of men 'who walk upon the earth'. Leaf notes the strong sound-patterning of the line (phrazeo... chazeo). Diomedes obeys, 'avoiding the wrath (mēnis) of Apollo', unlike Patroclus later. The scene restates the wisdom Dione has just voiced: 'he endureth not for long who fighteth with the immortals' (5.407), and it is answered in Book VI by Diomedes' tale of Lycurgus (6.128-41).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 1 (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1900), notes on 5.436-42 and 5.440-2

title: Apollo's wraith (eidolon) of Aeneas and the temple on Pergamus
short: Apollo carries Aeneas to his temple on Pergamus and leaves a phantom double on the field, over which both armies fight.
body: An eidōlon is a phantom or image (LSJ, citing this passage); the same word is used of the shades of the dead in the Odyssey (11.476). Apollo hides Aeneas in his temple on the citadel of Troy, where Leto and Artemis heal him in the 'great sanctuary' (aduton, a place not to be entered). Leaf points out that this temple and Athena's in Book VI are among the very few temples in Homer, and that the idea of an inner sanctum looks later than most Homeric religion. He also thought the wraith un-Homeric: it plays no further part, and nobody is surprised when the real Aeneas returns (5.512-18). He compares Stesichorus' famous story that only a phantom of Helen went to Troy, a version Plato reports (Phaedrus 243a-b) and Euripides dramatised in Helen.

title: Sarpedon's rebuke: 'caught in the meshes of all-ensnaring flax'
greek: ἀψῖσι λίνου ἁλόντε πανάγρου (hapsisi linou halonte panagrou)
short: Sarpedon, the Lycian ally, shames Hector by warning that the Trojans will be caught like fish or birds in a net and become prey for the enemy.
body: This is Sarpedon's first real entrance in the poem, and Leaf sketches him as the ideal aristocrat. He rebukes Hector for leaving the fighting to allies who, unlike the Trojans, have nothing of their own to defend at Troy. The image of the net (linon panagron, 'flax that catches everything'; hapsis, 'mesh', occurs only here in Homer) is unusual; Leaf observes that net-fishing appears elsewhere in Homer only in similes (Odyssey 22.383-6) and that the periphrasis sounds more Hesiodic or tragic than Homeric. The puzzling dual halonte ('you two being caught') was much discussed: Monro considers that it may refer distributively to Trojan men and their wives, or allude covertly to the absent Paris. The rebuke works: Hector leaps from his chariot (5.494). Rebuke speeches like this are a regular device for turning the tide of battle.

title: Simile: chaff on the threshing-floor
greek: ἱερὰς κατ᾽ ἀλωάς... ξανθὴ Δημήτηρ (hieras kat' alōas... xanthē Dēmētēr)
short: The Achaeans turn white with dust as chaff whitens around winnowers when 'fair-haired Demeter' separates grain from husk.
body: Winnowing was done by tossing threshed grain into the wind so that the light chaff blew away. The threshing-floors are 'sacred' (hieros) as places of Demeter's work; Leaf so takes it, while Monro suggests the older sense 'strong, goodly'. 'Fair-haired' (xanthē) Demeter, the corn goddess, is the colour of ripe grain and is herself pictured as separating the grain. The point of the comparison is visual: the dust kicked up by the rallying Trojan chariots settles on the Greeks until they are white like the chaff-heaps. Leaf notes another winnowing simile at 13.588-90 and leaves open whether a fan or natural wind is meant. Agricultural similes like this bring the world of peace into the middle of the fighting and make the destruction more vivid by contrast.

title: Apollo 'of the golden sword' (chrysaoros)
short: An old cult title of Apollo, 'with sword of gold', whose meaning puzzled ancient critics because Apollo fights with a bow, not a sword.
body: LSJ glosses chrusaoros as 'with sword of gold', used of Apollo here and at 15.256, of Demeter in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (4), and of Artemis in an oracle quoted by Herodotus (8.77). Leaf notes the surprise this caused: Apollo's weapon is the bow ('of the silver bow', 5.449). Some ancient grammarians argued that aor once meant any implement, so that the 'golden aor' could be Apollo's lyre or Demeter's winnowing fan; Leaf finds no evidence for such a sense and concludes that, like many archaic divine titles, its meaning is lost. The epithet is a useful reminder that Homeric epithets for gods often preserve cult language older than the poem, and should not always be read as descriptions of what the god does in the scene.

anchor: have shame each of the other
title: Aidos: 'be men, and have shame before each other'
greek: ἀλλήλους τ᾽ αἰδεῖσθε (allēlous t' aideisthe); αἰδώς (aidōs)
short: Agamemnon's exhortation defines aidos, the sense of shame before one's comrades, as the force that holds a battle line together.
body: Aidōs is the respect for others' opinion that makes a person ashamed to act badly; LSJ defines it as 'reverence, awe, respect for the feeling or opinion of others', and so 'shame, self-respect, sense of honour'. Agamemnon's logic is practical: where men feel shame before one another, more are saved than killed, while those who run win 'neither glory (kleos) nor any defence'. The same lines are spoken by Ajax at 15.561-4, where they open with 'put aidōs in your hearts'. Hera's cry 'Aidōs, Argives!' at 5.787 uses the noun as an exclamation, which Leaf explains as 'let there be shame in you', comparable to our 'For shame!'. Aidōs is the motive Hector gives Andromache for returning to battle: 'I have shame before the Trojans' (6.441-3). In the Iliad it is a social emotion, felt before particular people, rather than a private conscience.

title: Heracles' earlier sack of Troy
short: Tlepolemus boasts that his father Heracles once sacked Troy with only six ships, because King Laomedon cheated him of the promised horses.
body: Tlepolemus, son of Heracles and leader of the Rhodians (2.653-70), taunts Sarpedon with his father's earlier capture of Troy. Leaf explains the legend: Heracles rescued Laomedon's daughter Hesione from a sea-monster (the monster's wall appears at 20.145-8), and when Laomedon refused the promised reward, the divine horses of Tros, Heracles destroyed the city. Laomedon is the poem's model of a faithless king; he also cheated Poseidon and Apollo of their wages for building Troy's walls (21.441-57). Sarpedon's reply turns the story against Tlepolemus: Troy fell then because of Laomedon's folly (5.649-51). The duel is between a son and a grandson of Zeus (5.631), and Sarpedon wins, though Zeus 'as yet' saves him from death (5.662), a hint, Leaf notes, of his death at Patroclus' hands in Book XVI.

title: Hades 'of the famous horses' (klytopolos)
short: An epithet used in the Iliad only of Hades, perhaps reflecting the god's chariot in the abduction of Persephone or an old link between horses and death.
body: LSJ notes that klutopōlos, 'with noble steeds', is in the Iliad always an epithet of Hades (5.654, 11.445, 16.625). Leaf considers two explanations. It may simply mark Hades as a great king with splendid horses, like an earthly lord; or it may preserve a connection between the horse and the underworld, seen in Etruscan art, in the modern Greek figure of Charos riding, and in the story that Hades carried off Persephone in his chariot (Homeric Hymn to Demeter 17-20). Leaf also reports A. W. Verrall's objection that pōlos in Homer means 'foal' and his proposed alternative reading, which has not found acceptance. The formula sends Tlepolemus' 'soul' (psuchē) to the god of the dead and so frames the boast as a death sentence.

title: Sarpedon's swoon: the psyche leaves and returns
greek: τὸν δ᾽ ἔλιπε ψυχή... αὖτις δ᾽ ἐμπνύνθη (ton d' elipe psuchē... autis d' empnunthē)
short: When the spear is pulled from his thigh, Sarpedon's psyche 'leaves him' and mist covers his eyes, but the North Wind's breath revives him.
body: Homer describes a faint in the same language as death: the psuchē, the life-breath that survives as a shade, 'left him' and mist (achlus) poured over his eyes. But Sarpedon 'breathed again' (empnunthē, which Aristarchus read for the manuscripts' ampnunthē, 'recovered breath') as the North Wind 'brought back to life' (zōgrei) his spirit. Monro notes that zōgrei here means 'gave him life', unlike its usual sense 'take a prisoner alive' (6.46). The passage shows how closely the Homeric soul is tied to breath. It also anticipates Sarpedon's real death at 16.502-5, after which Sleep and Death carry his body home to Lycia (16.666-83). Sarpedon is laid under the oak of Zeus; Leaf doubts that this is the oak by the Scaean gate, since any oak was sacred to Zeus.

title: Hera's chariot
short: An ekphrasis of a divine chariot in which every wooden or leather part of a mortal car is made of precious metal.
body: The description follows the order of getting a chariot ready: Hebe fits the wheels on the axle, then the pole and yoke are attached. Leaf notes that early Greek, Assyrian and Egyptian chariots usually have four or six spokes; eight are rare, and the divine chariot naturally has the largest number. Everything normally made of wood or leather is here gold, silver, bronze or iron: golden felloes with bronze tyres, silver hubs, a silver pole, a golden yoke. The platform (diphros) is 'plaited tight' with gold and silver straps; Leaf compares the woven leather floors of Egyptian chariots, which gave a springy surface. The passage is largely repeated at 8.381-96, and some analysts thought it a late expansion. In battle Homeric heroes use the chariot mainly for transport, as Monro and Leaf explain at 5.227.

title: Athena arms: the aegis and the Gorgon head
greek: αἰγὶς θυσσανόεσσα (aigis thussanoessa); Γοργείη κεφαλή (Gorgeiē kephalē)
short: Athena puts on Zeus' tunic and the tasselled aegis, ringed by Rout and bearing Strife, Valour, Onset and the Gorgon's head.
body: The aegis, Zeus' terror-bringing shield or cape (2.446-51; made by Hephaestus, 15.308-10), receives its fullest description here. Athena drops her woven peplos and dresses in Zeus' chiton for war. Phobos (Rout) is set round the aegis 'as a crown', and in it are Eris (Strife), Alkē (Valour) and Iōkē (Onset), with the Gorgon's head, 'a portent of Zeus'. Monro admits it is unclear whether these are figures depicted on it or powers actually present. Leaf thought 5.739-44 among the latest lines in the book, since the Gorgon head is unknown in Greek art before the seventh century BC and the passage resembles Agamemnon's arming in Book XI. The golden helmet 'fitted with the men-at-arms of an hundred cities' is equally obscure: Monro takes it as decorated with figures of warriors; Leaf records but doubts the view that it alludes to the 'hundred cities' of Crete.

title: The Horai, gate-keepers of heaven
short: The Hours (Horai), goddesses of the seasons, keep the cloud-gates of heaven and Olympus, opening and shutting them.
body: The gates of heaven groan open 'of their own accord' (automatai) because the Hōrai, 'Seasons' or 'Hours', are entrusted with heaven and Olympus 'to throw open the thick cloud or shut it to'. Leaf remarks on the freedom of the imagery, by which a gate made of cloud still creaks on its hinges. In Hesiod the Horai are daughters of Zeus and Themis named Eunomia (Good Order), Dike (Justice) and Eirene (Peace), who watch over human works (Theogony 901-3). Their role as keepers of the weather fits the idea that the seasons bring sky and cloud in turn. The scene, repeated at 8.393-5, shows Olympus imagined as a mountain whose summit reaches into the sky; Leaf discusses the cosmology in his note on 5.753-4.

title: Stentor 'of the brazen voice'
short: Hera shouts in the likeness of Stentor, whose voice equalled fifty men's; the name gave English the word 'stentorian'.
body: Stentor is never mentioned again in Homer, and Leaf notes that there was no consistent ancient tradition about him: some made him a Greek herald, and a rationalising scholiast credited him with inventing a speaking-trumpet. The 'brazen' voice compares the sound to bronze; compare 18.222, where Akhilleus' voice is called 'brazen'. Leaf points out that the proverb was current by Aristotle's time: in the Politics (7.4, 1326b) he asks who could be herald to an over-large city 'unless he had the voice of Stentor'. Hera's speech opens with an exclamatory 'Aidōs!' ('Shame!') and calls the Argives 'fair in semblance only'. Her claim that the Trojans now fight 'at the hollow ships' is, Leaf and Monro note, rhetorical exaggeration borrowed from 13.107. Aristarchus held the Dardanian gate to be the same as the Scaean gate.

title: Tydeus at Thebes
short: Athena shames Diomedes with his father Tydeus, a small man but a fighter, who alone defeated the Cadmeans in contests when sent as envoy to Thebes.
body: Tydeus, son of Oeneus of Calydon, was one of the Seven against Thebes, the expedition led by Adrastus to restore Polynices. Before the war he went as envoy (angelos) to Thebes and, though alone, challenged the young Cadmeans to contests and beat them all. Agamemnon tells a fuller version, including the ambush Tydeus survived on the way back, at 4.370-400, and Athena's role as his helper is part of the story. The Thebes saga is the great earlier war behind the Iliad: Diomedes and Sthenelus belong to the Epigonoi, the sons who later took the city (4.405-10). Leaf and Monro discuss the difficult syntax of 5.802-8; Aristarchus rejected 5.808 as copied from 4.390 and out of place, since Athena here stresses her restraint of Tydeus. Paternal comparison is a standard method of exhortation in the Iliad.

title: The cap of Hades and the wounding of Ares
short: Athena makes herself invisible to Ares by putting on the 'cap of Hades'; Diomedes then wounds the war god, who bellows like ten thousand men.
body: The cap of Hades is a folk-tale cap of invisibility, mentioned only here in Homer. Leaf compares the German Tarnkappe and lists later references: Perseus wears it in the Hesiodic Shield (226-7), Aristophanes jokes about it (Acharnians 390), and Plato pairs it with the ring of Gyges (Republic 612b). He suggests the name Aïdēs was still felt to mean 'the Unseen', and that the poet may simply be using a proverbial way of saying that Athena made herself invisible. With Athena guiding the spear, Diomedes wounds Ares in the lower belly. Ares bellows as loud as nine or ten thousand warriors (repeated of Poseidon at 14.148-9); Leaf notes that the passage deliberately exaggerates the physical scale of the gods. Ares 'fared amid the clouds' like a dark storm-cloud (5.864-7).

anchor: Most hateful to me art thou
title: Zeus rebukes Ares
greek: ἔχθιστος δέ μοί ἐσσι θεῶν (echthistos de moi essi theōn)
short: Zeus calls Ares the most hateful of the gods, in words that echo Agamemnon's insult to Akhilleus in Book I.
body: Ares complains that Zeus favours Athena; Zeus answers with a scowl (hupodra idōn) and contempt: 'Most hateful to me art thou of all gods... for ever is strife dear to thee and wars and fightings.' Leaf refers to 1.176-7, where Agamemnon says almost exactly this to Akhilleus ('most hateful to me of the kings... for ever is strife dear to thee'). The echo links the war god with the hero whose wrath drives the poem and casts Ares' grievance as a parody of a human quarrel. Zeus blames Hera's 'unyielding spirit' for her son's nature but heals him because he is his own child; otherwise Ares would have been thrown 'lower than the sons of heaven', which Leaf and Monro take as an allusion to the Titans cast into Tartarus (compare 8.13-16, 8.478-81).

title: Simile: fig-juice curdling milk
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ὀπὸς γάλα λευκὸν ἐπειγόμενος συνέπηξεν (hōs d' hot' opos gala leukon epeigomenos sunepēxen)
short: Paeon heals Ares as quickly as fig sap curdles milk into cheese, a homely kitchen image for a divine miracle.
body: Opos is the milky sap of the fig tree, which was used as rennet to curdle milk for cheese. Leaf cites Roman parallels (the Latin lac ficulneum mentioned by Columella, Varro and Pliny) and notes that the juice of the plant lady's bedstraw was used the same way in rural England. The point of the comparison is speed: the liquid becomes solid 'as a man stirreth it', just as Ares' flowing blood instantly closes into sound flesh. Monro discusses the reading peritrephetai ('curdles') against the manuscripts' peristrephetai ('is whirled round'). The deflating homeliness of the simile suits the end of the book: the god who bellowed like ten thousand men is bathed by Hebe and sits beside Zeus 'exulting in his glory', a phrase Aristarchus thought inappropriate here (Leaf on 5.906).
